claims.text: Periodic potential pulses enhance ethanol oxidation performance relative to constant-potential operation.
The enhancement is caused by transient active sites generated through modulation of the catalyst surface oxidation state.
Controlled potential pulses can induce repeated oxidation and reduction of the catalyst surface.
The relevant structural mediator is transient formation and subsequent reduction of surface oxide species or associated dynamic restructuring.
A Pd catalyst can undergo reversible oxidation and return toward its initial metallic state over successive oxidation and reduction treatments.
Oxidation during a pulse increases the population of oxygenated active sites.
Oxygenated active sites modulate the binding energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The altered intermediate binding favors the full 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol oxidation pathway.
IrOsPtPdRhRu can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a 12-electron process.
The reduction portion of each pulse cycle returns the surface to a stable configuration.
Repeated reduction preserves catalyst durability while retaining the catalytic benefit of oxidation.
Potential pulsing will produce higher ethanol-oxidation current density than constant-potential operation.
Potential pulsing will lower the ethanol-oxidation overpotential relative to constant-potential operation.
Potential pulsing will improve product selectivity and generate activity peaks synchronized with oxidation pulses.
The proposed mechanism applies only when the electrochemical potential range permits reversible surface oxidation and reduction.
Excessively high potentials may cause catalyst degradation rather than beneficial reversible modulation.
The dynamic oxidation-state mechanism may fail in non-aqueous environments.
In situ XAFS can detect reversible changes in catalyst oxidation state and local structure.
